confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation was not yet obtained; I downloaded Akerman 2008 SILEWP 2008-006 from the Internet Archive copy and found the quotation verbatim in sec. 4 'Stress', p.14, exactly as cited, plus a supporting line on p.9. (2) Deciding source: a 2008 primary phonology sketch (SIL working paper, 16 pp) of the standard Huzhu/Donggou dialect by a fieldworker, with explicit position and correlates (pitch + loudness); appropriate and current. (3) Cross-check: Nugteren 2011 (LOT 289, open access, now saved) states pp.35/63/174 that all Shirongol/QG languages, Mongghul included, have word-final accent with reduction of unaccented non-final vowels — confirms 'fixed-dominant final' (final stress, non-strict because Akerman notes occasional non-contrastive exceptions). sources.citation: Akerman 2008, Mongghul phonology sketch, SILEWP 2008-006, sec. 4 Stress (the Internet Archive PDF, full section read)
sources.quote: As a rule, the stress is on the final syllable of the word. Occasionally, the stress falls elsewhere. In those cases, stress placement does not distinguish meanings of words; therefore, there is no need to mark stress in the orthography.

sources.citation: Åkerman, Vesa. 2008. Mongghul Phonology Sketch. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2008-006. Dallas: SIL International. 16 pp.
sources.quote: 'As a rule, the stress is on the final syllable of the word. Occasionally, the stress falls elsewhere. In those cases, stress placement does not distinguish meanings of words... Stress consists of higher pitch and greater loudness, relative to those of neighbouring unstressed syllables.'
sources.locator: sec. 4 Stress, p.14 (p.15); also sec. 2.2.1 p.9

sources.citation: Nugteren, Hans. 2011. Mongolic Phonology and the Qinghai-Gansu Languages. PhD dissertation, Leiden University. LOT Dissertation Series 289. Utrecht: LOT. 563 pp.
sources.quote: p.35: 'Word-final accent is shared by all QG languages.' p.63: 'In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable... The QG languages show vowel reductions in unaccented syllables.' p.174: 'the accent in the QG languages generally falls on the final syllable, which ... is another source of vowel lengthening in Mongghul and Eastern Yugur' (citing Poppe 1955 on Mongghul first-syllable lengthening in (C)VCV(C) stems with non-high V1 + high V2).
sources.locator: sec. 1.5.1.1 p.35; sec. 2.4.3 p.63; sec. 3.14.5 p.174; p.17 defines Shirongol = Mongghul, Mangghuer, Baoan, Kangjia, Dongxiang

sources.citation: Chuluu, Üjiyediin (Chaolu Wu). 1994. Introduction, Grammar, and Sample Sentences for Monguor. Sino-Platonic Papers 57. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania. 35 pp. (Glottolog ref 456624; based on Chenggeltei's Huzhu-dialect materials)
sources.quote: No stress-placement statement; only lists [ə] as the allophone of /a/ in a 'non-stressed syllable', ex. kadam ~ kədam 'wolf' (first syllable reduced, consistent with non-initial/final stress).
sources.locator: sec. II.1.3 vowel allophone table (p.2 of paper)
